### MARKET DEVELOPMENTS _Copper initially moves up early in the month, but settles into a declining trend_ Copper’s price patterns during February have generally set the bearish trends behind most other commodities and mirrored declining equity market indices. Ending January on a downward note at $3148/t ($1.43/lb), LME three-month prices edged up daily through to February 9th , reaching what has so far been the month’s high of $3561/t ($1.62/lb), or 13% up on that January 30th position. Three consecutive days of price correction brought us back down to sub$4000/t levels on the 12th , and profit-taking on the 13th once again tested the $3450/t mark ($1.56/lb). Such support could not hold out, though, and by the 20th the 3-mo price had succumbed to the weight of market fundamentals by falling to $3171/t ($1.44/lb). The initial rise during early February suggested that copper was intending to show a remarkable resilience to the generally bearish fundamentals hanging over all markets, almost to the point of offering a degree of preparedness to shrug off the signs of economic downturn. Indeed, even as we go to press, the potential for price support remains, as tenuous as it might appear. _Rumours of SRB buying sustain the market…_ _..culminating in the expectation that the Reserve would buy up to 700kt_ This month’s relative price strength really began with a rumour first picked up in late-January. While the market _back then_ was focusing on the bullish sentiments of anticipation of the annual re-weighting of the S&P GSCI and DJAIG commodity indexes, stockpiling by Chinese participants (taking advantage of the SHFE price arbitrage) ahead of the Chinese New Year late in the month, and the ongoing production curtailments, newswires began to report that the Chinese State Reserve Bureau (SRB) was intending to replenish its stocks of various metals, including copper, aluminium and zinc. Given the usually secretive nature of the SRB’s business, selling the rumour alone would have been sufficient to have seen the price move up. Certainly, at the prevailing price levels, the SRB would have viewed any stock replenishment as sound economic business, and so the logic was there to substantiate the rumour. Once that particular cat was out of the bag, the debate moved to the next level, asking how much material was the SRB interested in buying. Again, back in January, the figure of 1Mt _to be purchased_ was in the air, but it has since been generally agreed that the SRB has its sights on raising its copper stock _to_ 1Mt _from_ the currently-acknowledged level of 300kt. **MONTHLY INDEXED LME CASH METAL PRICES (January 2007 = 100)** 140

that the SRB has already secured contracts to purchase approximately 300kt of cathode during the first half of this year.  If so, this has already doubled what we believe was held in stock by the SRB at the turn of the year.  Furthermore, according to some estimates, the SRB has already _physically_ taken in 20% of this tonnage.  Suppliers are understood to be Latin American and European producers, plus one or two traders.  However, now that the initial rumour behind the purchases is indeed gaining ground, the SRB might not fully go through with its declared aim of buying an additional 400kt if prices respond as we would expect under such a scenario.  That said the SRB is also thought to have secured a paper long position in December for 100kt of copper at a price of $2800/t.  This effectively gives the Chinese entity added flexibility in securing physical copper under a higher price environment. 

Even so, we should place the SRB’s recent and _potential_ purchases into proper context.  Some observers have viewed the SRB’s stock re-building efforts within the narrow “Chinese-only” context.  That is, buying the additional 300-700kt of metal amounts to between 5% and 12% of domestic demand (which, fundamentally, is little better than flat right now), and under that view the belief is that the SRB purchases will be of minor interest only to the global market. However, for 2008 and 2009 our research leaves us showing a combined metal surplus of almost 1Mt of copper, and so if the SRB does go through with its purchasing programme this year, the inference is that it is essentially looking to absorb 70% of this.  Though unlikely, it is not impossible, but the effect of this move alone would lower the market's overall stocks to ~49 days as opposed to the 63 days that we show today for 2009, i.e. roughly on a par with last December, and we would expect this to have a meaningful impact on prices. 

Along with the SRB being seen in the market buying physical copper, we should also mention that the South Korean Public Procurement Service (PPS) has announced its intention to raise _total_ metals stocks by c.50kt this year to 206kt. However, the market took little notice, given that the increase will be spread across several metals; additionally, the PPS says it will sell 12% more metal this year than last (143kt _vs._ 127kt), without giving further details clarifying the relative importance to individual metals. 

The (only) other fundamental prop to prices has come from the steady trickle of supply-side announcements detailing mine closures.  Early on in the month, the International Copper Study Group (ICSG) said it had identified over 0.5Mt Cu

Including the recently announced plan to shut the 60kt/a Mufulira mine we estimate that the overall impact of closures to date is equivalent to 670kt/a Cu (see Production). _..but still insufficient to offset demand-side losses_ _ABMS data adequately sum up market performances everywhere_ _Consequently, Exchange stocks continue to rise…_ _..with Italy, Spain, Korea and the USA absorbing the lion’s share_ However, as with almost every other commodity, such supply restraint is deemed in the marketplace as coming too little too late, as the rate of fall-off in demand is outstripping supply adjustments by a considerable degree. Economic data continue to stream in that confirms how poor Q4 2008 was and how much weaker this current quarter could get. Historical records for industrial production contraction in Germany (-12% in December) and Japan (-20%) have been tested, and illustrate that no matter where you look, it is difficult to find any encouraging industrial news. Furthermore, with December’s OECD lead indicator even for China also now joining the ranks of those countries in negative territory, there is an increasing probability of the requirement for additional supply-side restraint. The latest preliminary data from the American Bureau of Metal Statistics (ABMS) tie in with such general economic commentary. Noting that, for the year as a whole, US apparent copper consumption fell by almost 12% on 2007, the ABMS also pointed out that the real pain came in the final quarter, which showed a 22% tailspin. Similarly, domestic shipments of wire rod fell by almost 10% yearon-year, and 21% during Q4. It will take producers yet more time to respond to these dramatic levels of demand decline, and the consequence of that disconnect has been one of the most rapid build-ups in visible stocks the copper market has seen in recent times. Opening the year at 342kt, stocks in LME warehouses have surged by over 60% to almost 550kt. Indeed, stocks increased every day this month, except the 17th , since end-January’s level of 491kt. Once again, the largest increase in deliveries occurred in Europe where stocks rose by c.30kt to 257kt. Leghorn in Italy and Spain’s Bilbao have been the preferred destinations again, rising to 57kt and 30kt from end-January’s 19kt and 12kt, respectively; Rotterdam’s intake has been rather restrained during the month, although at 116kt it cl

early represents the bulk of Europe’s holdings. Meanwhile, New Orleans port in the USA continues to absorb metal under the country’s manufacturing collapse, as stock there has increased from 83kt or so WEEKLY COPPER EXCHANGE STOCKS AND CASH LME PRICE

South Korean warehouses are also a reflection of poor off-take, with Busan and Gwangyang now holding 66kt between them, although these two centres also show the highest amounts of cancelled tonnage of all LME warehouses, at c.13kt. The increase in Comex stocks during February has been rather less dramatic, from 36.5kt (metric) at the end of last month to just over 38kt by the 23rd , but even this is also up by 22% since the start of the year. Meanwhile, refined copper stocks on China’s SHFE have edged _down_ as this month has progressed, given the buying pattern from the SRB, but even here stocks have trended up from end-January’s c.20kt to 30kt by February 23rd . In summary, the over-riding picture from Exchange-related copper stocks reveals an aggregated total today approaching 620kt, up by almost 60% since the start of the year. Under the twin circumstances of increasing stocks and rapidly shrinking industrial activity, we have detected little if any change in cathode premia across all markets since our last report. If any spot business is being done in Grade A metal, it has usually been as a consequence of lower _scrap_ volumes being generated during these times of plant closures; the rising tide of cathode in stock, provides a ready substitute for diminished scrap availability, especially standard grade cathode, which continues to be flat to LME or attract a slight discount of up to $20/t. _Comex stocks also up, but SHFE levels decline under SRB purchasing_ _Premia little change under low business activity and rising stocks_ With our prior comments on the likely deteriorating industrial performance that lies ahead, it is not surprising that we continue to expect further increases in visible stock levels, higher stock days of consumption and, consequently, a tough time for prices in the near-term. From a fundamental perspective our supply/demand balance for 2009 and 2010 remain practically unchanged from last month. ### CONSUMPTION _IP data confirm scale of economic collapse_ _US stimulus package passes into law_ The latest round of economic indicators has reinforced the negative outlook for the global economy and copper consumption. Economic indicators from around the world are showing a rapid contraction in manufacturing activity. In Japan December’s industrial pro

duction (IP) posted a month-on-month decline of 9.6% and a horrendous 22.5% decline in year-on-year terms. In Germany, the declines were smaller, although at 4.6% in month-on-month terms and 12.4% in year-on-year terms they show how much activity is falling in what was Europe’s manufacturing powerhouse. In the US, January’s IP figure fell by 1.8% in monthon-month terms and concluded the sixth consecutive month of contraction. Although the Lunar New Year holiday tends to distort Chinese economic data in January and February, the near 19% decline in imports is a cause for concern. This and other negative economic data underlines the grim outlook for the global economy and copper consumption, and we maintain our forecast that copper consumption will fall by 4.6% to 17.1Mt in 2009 and will grow by just 1% in 2010 to 17.3Mt. After tense negotiations in the US senate and congress, President Obama has signed the $787Bn stimulus package into law, raising hopes that the US economy will start to recover in the second half of 2009 and strengthen further _February 2009_ _Page 6_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook Hunt_ in 2010. It is still too early to calculate the impact of the stimulus. However, what is clear is that for metals the near-term impact will be rather limited and it is not until 2010 that the package will start to have a significant direct impact on copper demand. The earliest effects of the package on the US consumer will be tax breaks of various sorts including a refundable tax credit of up to $400 for individuals and $800 for couples in 2009 and 2010. The tax breaks during last summer were a factor in the manufacturing PMI picking up during the summer months. But the rapid deterioration of the economy in general, and the job market in particular, means that consumers are much more likely to save the cash or use it to pay down debt rather than spend it. The steep drop in the US manufacturing PMI (see chart below) since August 2008 only underlines the scale of the task facing the US government. _Tax breaks unlikely to have major impact…_ #### **US MANUFACTURING PURCHASING MANAGERS INDEX** 65

While the tax breaks are likely to have a limited impact on US copper demand in 2009, other parts of the stimulus package will play a more significant role. The package includes $120Bn in infrastructure spending, including $27.5Bn for highway projects, $8.4Bn on public transportation, $9.3Bn on Amtrak and highspeed rail projects, $7.2Bn to improve access to high-speed internet. Further stimulus for copper consumption will come from energy spending which includes $11Bn in spending and loan guarantees for 4,800km of transmission lines; $6Bn of loan guarantees for renewable energy and transmission projects and other me

asures to improve the energy efficiency of federal buildings.  Projects such as these will partially counteract the fall in copper consumption caused by the downturn in the residential and non-residential construction sectors. However, the main copper end-uses in the US – construction (48% of national consumption) and automotive (28%) - will require the return of consumer and business confidence before there is a significant pick-up in US demand. 

The latest economic news has underlined the parlous state of the US economy and demonstrated the need for the government to provide economic stimulus. The US automotive industry remains headline news, with both GM and Chrysler asking for further government funding during the month to prevent bankruptcy. GM asked for $16.6Bn, on top of the $13.4Bn it has already received, and Chrysler requested an additional $5bn, which would take its total government loans to $9Bn.  The requests came as both companies unveiled restructuring plans, including job losses and plant closures, in an effort to cut costs and survive the economic downturn.  GM plans to cut 47,000 jobs, almost 20% of its

total global workforce, and has warned that its wholly-owned subsidiary, Swedish auto producer Saab, may be bankrupt by the month end if the Swedish government does not provide $568M in funding to keep it afloat until early 2010. 

Chrysler, meanwhile, is to cut 3000 jobs this year and reduce production by 100K units.  The two producers have estimated that the combined cost of their bankruptcies to the US government would amount to $125Bn, making their total bailout requests of $39Bn seem cheap in comparison.  Both companies have reached preliminary agreements with the United Auto Workers union to bring labour costs in line with those of Japanese auto producers operating in the US. If ratified, 91,000 hourly-paid employees will be impacted. 

GM now forecasts that US car sales will total 10.5M in 2009, down from its previous estimate of 12M.  US car and light vehicle output totalled 8.7M units in 2008, 20% lower than in 2007.  Output in January was at an annualised rate of 3.3M units, down from 6.6M units in December 2008 and around 10M units a year ago, reflecting the rapid decline of demand for new vehicles. 

_Housing starts hit fresh postwar low_ 

_White goods shipments continue their decline_ 

According to the US Census Bureau, housing starts fell to a new post-war low in January with the seasonally-adjusted annual rate sliding to 466,000 units, a month-on-month decline of 17% and a year-on-year decline of 56%.  The decline in housing permits was not as precipitous as that for starts, but still fell by 4.8% in month-on-month terms and was 51% lower in year-on-year terms.  The only positive that can be taken from this latest data is that it should help

draw down inventories for new homes which stand at a record high of almost 13 months. 

The collapse in the housing market has hit white goods producers hard. According to the Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers (AHAM), shipments of US-built and imported major home appliances fell by 9% in 2008, following a 6.2% drop in 2007.  Whirlpool, one of the world’s largest manufacturers of home appliances, said in its latest quarterly report that North American demand for its products will fall by 10%, and noted that US demand for home appliances had fallen by 11M units since 2005 to around 36M units – the lowest level since 1998.  Elsewhere in the world Whirlpool is forecasting that white goods demand will fall by 8% in Europe, and in Latin America and Asia demand will be flat to 5% lower.  The demand weakness has forced the company to close 5 plants and lay-off 5,000 workers globally.

After contracting by 8.4% in 2008 to 2Mt, we forecast that the rapid and ongoing deterioration of the US economy will result in US copper consumption contracting by a further 10.1% in 2009 to 1.8Mt.  We expect demand to bottom out in 2010 with a modest decline year-on-year of 1%, to 1.78Mt, before picking up again in 2011. 

One indication of just how poor the copper market in the USA is came at the end of last year, when Freeport confirmed the closure of its Hawthorne rod mill near Chicago.  The facility produced 120kt of rod last year and accounted for c.15% of group output.  Having already cut copper output throughout the chain, from mine to refinery, Freeport’s three other US-based rod facilities will not be required to cover for the loss of Hawthorne, and we expect a near 20% decline in group wire rod production this year over 2008, to c.620kt. 

In Europe, the initial plunge in economic activity in the wake of the Lehman Brothers failure appears to have slowed, the eurozone PMI in January rose fractionally from 33.9 in December to 34.4 in January.  However, this respite will prove short-lived amid concerns a number of major banks are potentially facing large losses because of expected defaults on loans made in a number of East European countries. 

It had been hoped that Eastern European growth would prove relatively resilient in the face of the global downturn.  However, the tightening of credit and the impact that this has had at all levels has undermined consumer and business confidence and exacerbated the impact of falling demand in Western Europe for eastern Europe’s manufactured goods.  This has resulted in the Czech Republic sliding into recession and it is likely to be joined by a number of other East European countries in the coming months. 

German car and light vehicle production totalled 6.1M units for the year, 2.2% lower than a year ago.  In the UK, output fell by 5.8% year on year, to total 1.6M units for 2008.  BMW has cut 850 jobs at its Oxfordshire Min

i plant in the UK and output has been reduced from a seven- to a five-day week.  French car and light vehicle output fell by 16.1% in 2008, to 2.5M units, with production in December down by 64% year on year.  In Spain, total vehicle output was 12.1% lower year on year, at 2.5M units, and Italian production fell by 18.5% in the eleven months to November 2008, to 990K units (latest figures available). 

With many of the European copper semis sector dependent on the performance of the automotive industry, it was no surprise for us to learn that in general rod and wire suppliers are thought to be operating thus far into 2009 at 70% or so of last year’s level, with one supplier noting that in some cases orders were down even more (by 50%) during the final quarter last year.  Meanwhile, copper shapes deliveries are believed to be down by a near 20-25% across the board. One semis producer who is not so dependent on autos says his plant is still operating at 85% of last year’s level, supported by the power sector that has not been as badly hit so far this year as have both autos and construction. 

The quarterly results call from Germany’s Aurubis (formerly Norddeutsche Affinerie) summarised the widespread position adequately when it referred to a “..general economic slowdown leaving its mark since November”.  This has forced companies, including Aurubis, into extending year-end holiday periods and reducing temporary employee levels, both resulting in lower output during the last quarter over Q4 2007.  Furthermore, Aurubis will discontinue continuous casting at Olen, suggesting that the company does not anticipate any significant improvement for some time. 

Comments such as these all point to another difficult year ahead for Western European copper demand.  After suffering a 5% year-on-year decline last year, we anticipate a near 10% reduction in demand this year as well to just 3.14Mt, taking us back to levels last seen in 1990.

Similarly, market conditions in Japan have gone from bad to worse, according to most economic and industrial indicators.  The Japanese Copper and Brass Association’s (JCBA) December report put that month’s output at just 57.8kt, which is effectively at a level pre-1985.  Q4 p

roduction of just 206kt was 12% below Q3 and 19.5% lower than the same period of 2007. Most severely affected was copper strip, where output of c.13kt or so mirrored levels last seen in Q2 1992. Equally, brass bar continued its sharp decline at just 14.6kt for the month, 1.3kt off November’s prior all-time low and over 21% below the level of December 2007. But worse news came in January, when preliminary data from the JCBA showed that output of rolled copper products fell 20% month-on-month to just 46kt. This was 45% lower than a year ago and the lowest figure since the summer of 1975. A similar data set came from the Japanese Copper Wire and Cable Association, which put January’s shipments of just 53.1kt over 21% lower than a year ago, and at levels on a par with December 1975. _The slight rise in 2008 vehicle output fails to boost confidence…_ _..with IP contracting by unprecedented levels in December_ _Copper demand unlikely to recover before 2011_ On a (slightly more) positive note Japanese, car and light vehicle output increased in 2008, albeit by a meagre 0.7%, to 11.7M units, higher than US output for the third consecutive year. This accounts for the “relative” strength shown in the automotive wire and cable sector, in which shipments increased by 1%. However, Japanese producers are not immune to the downturn with Toyota forecasting its first loss in 71 years of $3Bn in March, and redundancies expected shortly. Japan’s third largest producer, Nissan, announced during the month that it is to cut 20,000 jobs in an effort to contain costs, and is considering shifting some of its domestic production to cheaper overseas locations. Honda is still expecting a profit for the fiscal year to March 31st 2009, albeit at less than previously expected levels. Outside the automotive sector, Japanese industry in general is contracting and this appears to be an accelerating trend. In November 2008 Japanese industrial production plunged by 8.5% in month-on-month terms and was down by 13.7% in year-on-year terms. However, December’s figure surpassed expectations posting month-on-month and year-on-year declines of 9.6% and 22.5% respectively. We expect that demand across all markets will continue to weaken further this year as both overseas and domestic orders continue to fall. Thus we project that Japanese refined copper consumption will fall by 15.8% in 2009 to just above 1Mt, and it will do well, we believe to hold at around this level during 2010. _Page 10_ _February 2009_ _Copper Metal Service_ _Brook

_Central Africa to remain significant supplier to the spot concentrates market during 2009_

According to official customs statistics China’s January copper concentrate imports were 505kdmt which was virtually flat (-0.37%) on the same period last year.  Chile remains the largest supplier (28.5%) followed by Peru (14.5%), Australia (12.5%) and Mexico (12%).  New participants (relative to last year) include Laos (Phu Kham) and the Dominican Republic (Cerro de Maimon).  As mentioned, a perceived easing of the country’s acid bottleneck, coupled with the ongoing benefits of the favourable SHFE:LME price arbitrage have helped maintain spot concentrate buying interest.  In addition, the reintroduction of “tolling trade”, whereby the larger smelters will be exempt from taxes and duties associated with importing concentrates and exporting metal, as well as being protected from any price arbitrage exposure, should encourage these smelters to operate at higher utilisation rates and also reduce the volatility on imports from month to month.  However, there appears to be some uncertainty as to how much of each smelter’s imported feed will be regulated under this trading system although it is likely to be ~20% of the total.  Our feeling is that there will be further downward pressu

re on spot TC/RCs in China given the distinct lack of scrap and blister availability and also given that the oxygen plant at the large (and expanding) Guixi smelter is now repaired and the strong performance of the new 100kt/a Dongying plant that was commissioned in December 2008. 

There have been a number of developments within central Africa that are worthy of note and that will have an impact on the global custom copper concentrate market.  Firstly, there have been various changes to smelting capacity in Zambia with the commissioning of the new 150kt/a Chambishi plant last month.  In addition, Vedanta has announced that it is phasing out its 110kt/a (effective capacity) Nkana smelter now that its new 300kt/a Chingola smelter is operational (this was commissioned in Q4 last year).  Also, towards the end of last year Equinox Minerals opened its 170kt/a Lumwana mine.  Lack of smelting capacity in central Africa during 2008 led to the export of significant quantities of concentrates (primarily from the Frontier mine in DRC and Kansanshi mine in Zambia).  We estimate that last year more than 450kdmt of concentrates were shipped from these countries to offshore smelters.  For 2009, there will be a full year of production from Lumwana while both of the new smelters will be in ramp up mode.  Meanwhile, Mopani is to close its 45kt/a Mufulira mine in March, freeing up 100kt/a of concentrate space in the Mufulira smelter.  Assuming each of the new smelters achieve their target ramp up expectations, the net outflow of concentrates from this region is projected to be somewhat below 400kt in 2009 with the risk being to the upside of this figure.  The Chinese owners of the new Chambishi smelter plan to embark on a study to further expand the plant, although no specific tonnage target has been released. 

The long-term Mating Season is beginning to wind down with many buyers and sellers having accepted the $75/t & 7.5c/lb benchmark established between Freeport and its Japanese counterparts at the end of last year.  Both Freeport and Escondida have concluded all of their settlements, while the same is apparently true of Los Pelambres and Ok Tedi.  However, not all of the other negotiations have been straightforward.  There appear to be unresolved issues amongst a number of Asian smelters as to whether the $75/t & 7.5c/lb benchmark is an appropriate level for several producers of high-gold bearing copper concentrates.  This is perhaps a little surprising given that both Grasberg and Ok Tedi are classified in this category and have already established terms at these levels.  Elsewhere, several contracts involving Highland Valley apparently remain outstanding, notably in Japan.  We would imagine that as one of the few remaining producers of high-grade copper concentrates (~39% Cu) the Canadian miner will be seeking a premium in its long-term TC/RCs to reflect this.

No. 2 scrap remains extremely tight in most markets, reflecting the low copper price and greatly reduced manufacturing activity.  In the US, this situation became evident in November last year with scrap exports plummeting by more than 30% month on month to 50.4kt and then falling further, to 47.9kt, in December.  During the first ten months of 2008, monthly exports from the US averaged 81kt.  Overall shipments for last year were 908kt (906kt in 2007) with 75% (73%) of this absorbed by China and Hong Kong.  According to Chinese custom statistics the country’s scrap imports remained subdued during January 2009, having declined by 56% year on year.  That said the country’s appetite for No.2 grades remains strong which has been reflected in a further decline in US spreads for this quality which have again narrowed, from 16c/lb below April Comex last month to 12c/lb under May Comex during the last week of February.

### PRODUCTION NEWS 

Following a barrage of mine closures over the past three months, the number of new announcements has tailed off markedly.  The only significant casualty that came to light this month was Mopani’s 60kt/a Mufulira mine in Zambia which is to close next month.  In reality, output had fallen to 40-45kt/a Cu in recent years and this is the higher cost of the company’s two underground operations (the other being Nkana which has the added benefit of a cobalt by-product credit). As mentioned in the CONCENTRATE MARKETS section the loss of this mine will free up 100kt/a of concentrate smelting capacity at Mopani’s Mufulira smelter which, in turn, will help alleviate the smelter bottleneck in central Africa. Elsewhere, Freeport McMoran has closed its Morenci mill for the loss of approximately 50kt/a of copper-in-concentrates.  This follows the closure of the company’s 50kt/a Chino mill late last year and will, no doubt, lead to much lower production at the company’s Miami smelter this year.  Last year the plant is estimated to h

ave produced a little over 200kt Cu while for 2009 we expect the figure to fall to ~150kt Cu.  Taking account of all known closures and curtailments we now estimate that the overall decline in mine output, to date, is equivalent to 670kt/a Cu.

Inmet Mining expects to be producing metal from its 72kt/a Las Cruces mine in Spain by the end of April this year.  Last May the company suffered a setback when authorisation was not granted fo

r the dewatering and re-injection system of the project.
